inputs.original_text: The Punjab and Haryana High Court granted regular bail to a man booked under national-security provisions and the Official Secrets Act, based on allegations that he was in telephone contact with Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri.” That is not an acquittal—but neither should a security label turn suspicion into proof. The call to ensure courts don’t leave “genuine security threats” free risks putting state anxieties ahead of basic rights. Governments must protect people by building credible cases and respecting due process, not by treating contact or association as guilt. Security laws need scrutiny precisely because unchecked state power can harm the people least able to defend themselves.
inputs.modified_text: The Punjab and Haryana High Court granted regular bail to a man accused under national-security provisions and the Official Secrets Act, based on allegations of telephone contact with Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri.” Bail is not an acquittal, but it is a reminder that suspicion and security rhetoric cannot replace evidence. When governments are urged to keep “genuine security threats” from being released, the danger is that ordinary people’s rights become expendable in the name of state anxiety. That power rarely falls evenly: people with fewer resources are often least able to challenge accusations or defend themselves. Protecting the public means building credible cases and respecting due process—not treating contact or association as proof of guilt.
